lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 7 you met the 6 Rs. Can you name three? (Rethink, refuse, reduce, reuse, repair, recycle.) Today: designing products so that nothing becomes waste.
A linear economy takes, makes and throws away. A circular economy keeps products and materials in use as long as possible, and returns natural materials safely to the soil.
Technical loops keep products going: maintain and repair, reuse and share, refurbish and remanufacture, and last of all recycle. The smaller the loop, the more value and energy is saved.
Biological loops return natural materials to nature: food waste and plant-based materials are composted or turned into biogas, and feed new crops.
Design for repair and disassembly: screws instead of glue, standard parts, spare parts and repair guides. Modules swap out, and parts come apart into single materials for recycling.
Cost per year shows real value. A 20-gold kettle lasting 2 years costs 20 ÷ 2 = 10 gold a year. A 45-gold kettle lasting 9 years costs 45 ÷ 9 = 5 gold a year.
New ideas keep things in use: renting, sharing, take-back schemes and repair cafés. Since 2021, right to repair laws in the UK and the EU make some appliances' makers supply spare parts for years.

Try it in the world: mend something with a grown-up, or plan a swap shop in your village. In LIFE, the Tool Book shows the sandpaper and the pliers, for mending and refinishing. Next: future technology.

exercises.prompt: A linear economy is take, make, throw away.
exercises.hint: Picture a straight line with no way back.
exercises.explain: True: linear means materials go one way, to waste; circular keeps them going round.

exercises.prompt: Which loop keeps the most value in a product?
exercises.hint: The smaller the loop, the more is saved.
exercises.explain: Keeping a product working keeps all its parts, energy and value; recycling keeps only the materials.

exercises.prompt: Match each loop to an example.
matches: fixing up old laptops to resell
exercises.hint: Kept going, passed on, made like new, or melted down?
exercises.explain: Maintain: oiling. Reuse: passing a coat on. Refurbish: laptops made like new. Recycle: cans melted.

exercises.prompt: A 30-gold lamp lasts 6 years. What does it cost per year?
exercises.hint: Share the price by the years it lasts.

exercises.prompt: A technical or a biological material?
exercises.hint: Can it rot safely back into the soil?
exercises.explain: Biological: peel and leaves, which rot. Technical: glass, phones and cans, kept going by technical loops.

exercises.prompt: Label the loops: tap a word, then its number.
exercises.hint: The smallest technical loop is nearest the middle; the biological loop is on the left.
exercises.explain: From the smallest technical loop out: maintain, then refurbish, then recycle, the biggest. Compost is the biological loop, back to the soil.

exercises.prompt: Which design is easiest to repair?
choices: held together with screws, with spare parts
exercises.hint: Could you open it with ordinary tools?
exercises.explain: Screws let you open it, and spare parts let you fix it.

exercises.prompt: Kettle A costs 24 gold and lasts 2 years; kettle B costs 60 gold and lasts 10 years. How much less per year does B cost?
exercises.hint: Work out each one's cost per year, then subtract.
exercises.explain: A: 24 ÷ 2 = 12 a year. B: 60 ÷ 10 = 6 a year. 12 − 6 = 6 gold less a year.

exercises.prompt: Glue makes a product easier to take apart.
exercises.hint: Think about what glue is for.
exercises.explain: False: glue makes parts hard to separate; screws and clips make disassembly easy.

exercises.prompt: Easy to repair, or hard to repair?
exercises.hint: Can it be opened, and can you get the parts and the know-how?
exercises.explain: Easy: a swappable battery, a repair guide, unclipping parts. Hard: a sealed battery, no spare parts.

choices: rebuilding used products as good as new
exercises.hint: It is one of the technical loops, bigger than reuse.
exercises.explain: Remanufacturing rebuilds used products, like engines, so they work as new: a loop that saves the parts.

exercises.prompt: Over 12 years: a 15-gold toaster lasts 3 years, or a 40-gold one lasts all 12. How much more do the cheap ones cost in all?
exercises.hint: How many cheap ones are needed? Add up their cost, then compare.

exercises.prompt: A sofa's cover is torn, but its frame is strong. What is the best choice?
choices: replace the cover, keep the sofa
exercises.hint: Choose the smallest loop that still works.
exercises.explain: Replacing only the cover keeps the strong frame in use: maintain and repair saves the most.

exercises.prompt: Right to repair laws make some appliances' makers supply spare parts for years.
exercises.hint: Think about the laws the lesson named, from 2021.
exercises.explain: True: since 2021, UK and EU rules mean makers of some appliances, like washing machines, must supply spare parts for years.

exercises.prompt: Match each idea to how it keeps things in use.
exercises.hint: Who uses or mends the product in each idea?
exercises.explain: Renting shares one item; take-back lets makers reuse parts; repair cafés mend; tool libraries lend.

exercises.prompt: Which material choice makes recycling easiest?
exercises.hint: Recycling needs materials that can be sorted.
exercises.explain: A single labelled plastic can be sorted and recycled; mixed, glued or coated materials can't be separated.
